claim: The cerebellar vermis has been implicated in a surprising range of neuropsychiatric disorders and cognitive and affective functions.
source: The cerebellar vermis, long associated with axial motor control, has been implicated in a surprising range of neuropsychiatric disorders and cognitive and affective functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations in the introduction referencing prior literature on vermis involvement in various disorders and functions.

claim: Five major classes of glutamatergic projection neurons in the mouse fastigial nucleus are distinguished by gene expression, morphology, distribution, and input-output connectivity.
source: Here, using single-cell gene expression profiling and anatomical circuit analyses of vermis output neurons in the mouse fastigial (medial cerebellar) nucleus, we identify five major classes of glutamatergic projection neurons distinguished by gene expression, morphology, distribution, and input-output connectivity.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript including single-cell qPCR, immunostaining, and circuit tracing experiments.

claim: Each fastigial cell type is connected with a specific set of Purkinje cells and inferior olive neurons.
source: Each fastigial cell type is connected with a specific set of Purkinje cells and inferior olive neurons and in turn innervates a distinct collection of downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde and anterograde tracing experiments shown in Figure 7 and related data.

claim: Each fastigial cell type innervates a distinct collection of downstream targets.
source: Each fastigial cell type is connected with a specific set of Purkinje cells and inferior olive neurons and in turn innervates a distinct collection of downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde and transsynaptic tracing experiments shown in Figures 3-6.

claim: Transsynaptic tracing indicates extensive disynaptic links with cognitive, affective, and motor forebrain circuits.
source: Transsynaptic tracing indicates extensive disynaptic links with cognitive, affective, and motor forebrain circuits.
evidence: This claim is supported by AAV1-mediated transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Diverse cerebellar vermis functions could be mediated by modular synaptic connections of distinct fastigial cell types with posturomotor, oromotor, positional-autonomic, orienting, and vigilance circuits.
source: These results indicate that diverse cerebellar vermis functions could be mediated by modular synaptic connections of distinct fastigial cell types with posturomotor, oromotor, positional-autonomic, orienting, and vigilance circuits.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation based on the connectivity data presented throughout the manuscript and summarized in Figure 8.

claim: The cerebellum has been implicated in several cognitive functions and neuropsychiatric disorders.
source: The cerebellum has been implicated in several cognitive functions and neuropsychiatric disorders, which are more typically associated with the cerebral cortex and basal ganglia (Tsai et al., 2012; Hariri, 2019; Schmahmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Nonmotor functions of the cerebellum are widely assumed to be mediated by the cerebellar hemispheres and their connections with the thalamus.
source: Although it is widely assumed that such nonmotor functions are mediated by the cerebellar hemispheres and their connections with the thalamus (Strick et al., 2009; Buckner, 2013; Wang et al., 2014; De Schutter, 2019), increasing functional and anatomical evidence points to roles for the vermis (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Watson et al., 2009; Halko et al., 2014; Watson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2017; Badura et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018; Albazron et al., 2019; Brady et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Increasing functional and anatomical evidence points to roles for the vermis in nonmotor functions.
source: Although it is widely assumed that such nonmotor functions are mediated by the cerebellar hemispheres and their connections with the thalamus (Strick et al., 2009; Buckner, 2013; Wang et al., 2014; De Schutter, 2019), increasing functional and anatomical evidence points to roles for the vermis (Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Watson et al., 2009; Halko et al., 2014; Watson et al., 2014; Zhang et al., 2016; Wagner et al., 2017; Badura et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018; Albazron et al., 2019; Brady et al., 2019; Watson et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The vermis is an evolutionarily old portion of the cerebellum best known for its influence on brainstem circuits for posture and eye movements.
source: an evolutionarily old portion of the cerebellum best known for its influence on brainstem circuits for posture and eye movements (Chambers and Sprague, 1955; Ohtsuka and Noda, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Structural and functional abnormalities of the vermis have been associated with various psychiatric disorders and conditions, including autism, schizophrenia, mood disorders, chronic pain, and addiction.
source: Structural and functional abnormalities of the vermis have been associated with various psychiatric disorders and conditions, including autism, schizophrenia, mood disorders, chronic pain, and addiction (Weinberger et al., 1980; Courchesne et al., 1988; Sweeney et al., 1998; Strakowski et al., 2005; Andreasen and Pierson, 2008; Moulton et al., 2010; Fatemi et al., 2012; Moulton et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The cerebellum is thought to be organized in parallel circuit modules that comprise specific sets of inferior olive neurons, Purkinje cells, and vestibular or cerebellar nucleus neurons.
source: The cerebellum is thought to be organized in parallel circuit modules that comprise specific sets of inferior olive (IO) neurons, Purkinje cells (PCs), and vestibular or cerebellar nucleus neurons (Oscarsson, 1979; Ito, 1984; Apps and Hawkes, 2009; Voogd, 2011; Apps et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The cerebellar vermis, caudal medial accessory olive, and fastigial nucleus collectively constitute the broad 'A' module.
source: The cerebellar vermis, caudal medial accessory olive, and fastigial nucleus (FN; medial cerebellar nucleus) collectively constitute the broad 'A' module (Groenewegen and Voogd, 1977), which is likely to include several submodules (Apps, 1990; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The broad 'A' module is likely to include several submodules.
source: The cerebellar vermis, caudal medial accessory olive, and fastigial nucleus (FN; medial cerebellar nucleus) collectively constitute the broad 'A' module (Groenewegen and Voogd, 1977), which is likely to include several submodules (Apps, 1990; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The fastigial nucleus has been implicated in diverse motor and nonmotor functions in human imaging studies.
source: Although the fastigial nucleus has been implicated in diverse motor and nonmotor functions in human imaging studies (Schmahmann, 1991; Schmahmann, 1998; Albazron et al., 2019), its small size (Diedrichsen et al., 2011; Tellmann et al., 2015) has precluded precise functional localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The small size of the fastigial nucleus has precluded precise functional localization in human imaging studies.
source: Although the fastigial nucleus has been implicated in diverse motor and nonmotor functions in human imaging studies (Schmahmann, 1991; Schmahmann, 1998; Albazron et al., 2019), its small size (Diedrichsen et al., 2011; Tellmann et al., 2015) has precluded precise functional localization.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mono- and multi-synaptic connections with the midbrain, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex are likely to mediate vermis and fastigial influences on affective and cognitive functions.
source: Mono- and multi-synaptic connections with the midbrain, hippocampus, basal ganglia, and cerebral cortex are likely to mediate vermis and fastigial influences on affective and cognitive functions (Steriade, 1995; Teune et al., 2000; Watson et al., 2014; Badura et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018; Watson et al., 2019; Vaaga et al., 2020)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature and represents an inference about functional implications.

claim: The specific fastigial cell types responsible for influences on affective and cognitive functions are not known.
source: but the specific fastigial cell types responsible for these influences are not known.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: The diverse motor and nonmotor functions of the cerebellar vermis are mediated by multiple types of fastigial output neurons with distinct circuit connections.
source: In this study, we hypothesized that the diverse motor and nonmotor functions of the cerebellar vermis are mediated by multiple types of fastigial output neurons with distinct circuit connections.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the study.

claim: Several molecularly and anatomically distinct types of excitatory projection neurons exist in the mouse fastigial nucleus.
source: By combining single-cell gene expression, immunohistochemical, and circuit connectivity analyses, we identified several molecularly and anatomically distinct types of excitatory projection neurons in the mouse fastigial nucleus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Fastigial cell types exhibit segregated, modular circuit connectivity.
source: Anterograde, transsynaptic, and retrograde tracing analyses indicate segregated, modular circuit connectivity; each fastigial cell type is linked with a specific set of PCs and IO neurons and makes divergent projections to functionally-related downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by the circuit tracing data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific fastigial cell types are linked with circuits responsible for distinct aspects of cerebellar motor and nonmotor functions.
source: Disynaptic connections with the basal ganglia, basal forebrain, and cerebral cortex revealed that specific fastigial cell types are linked with circuits responsible for distinct aspects of cerebellar motor and nonmotor functions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the transsynaptic tracing data and represents an interpretation of the functional implications.

claim: The fastigial nucleus is the medial cluster of cerebellar nucleus neurons.
source: The fastigial nucleus (FN) is the medial cluster of cerebellar nucleus neurons (Dow, 1942), delineated in mammals by surrounding white matter (Larsell, 1970).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The fastigial nucleus comprises at least three subdivisions: a rostral part, a caudal part, and a dorsolateral protuberance.
source: Despite its small size, the FN comprises at least three subdivisions (Korneliussen, 1968; Beitz and Chan-Palay, 1979): a rostral part, a caudal part, and a dorsolateral protuberance (DLP), which is well developed in rodents (Fujita et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each subdivision of the fastigial nucleus has been linked with distinct sets of Purkinje cells, inferior olive subnuclei, and downstream brain regions.
source: Each of these subdivisions have been linked with distinct sets of Purkinje cells, inferior olive subnuclei, and downstream brain regions (Batton et al., 1977; Teune et al., 2000; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007; Sugihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Antibodies for SPP1, SNCA, and CALB2 reliably labeled specific subsets of neurons that were located predominantly in distinct subregions of the fastigial nucleus.
source: Antibodies for SPP1 (osteopontin), SNCA (alpha-synuclein), and CALB2 (calretinin) reliably labeled specific subsets of neurons that were located predominantly in distinct subregions of the FN (Figure 1; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: SPP1-immunopositive neurons were prominent in the caudal portion of the DLP and were sparsely distributed ventrally in caudal regions of the fastigial nucleus.
source: In caudal regions of the FN (Figure 1B), SPP1-immunopositive (SPP1+) neurons were prominent in the caudal portion of the DLP (cDLP) and were sparsely distributed ventrally.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SNCA+ neurons were prominent ventrally in the caudal fastigial nucleus, but were sparse in the cDLP.
source: In contrast SNCA+ neurons were prominent ventrally in the caudal fastigial nucleus (cFN), but were sparse in the cDLP.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The majority of neurons in rostral regions of the fastigial nucleus were SPP1+.
source: In rostral regions of the FN (Figure 1C), the majority of neurons were SPP1+.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Neurons strongly immunopositive for CALB2 were prominent rostrally in ventral and lateral parts of the fastigial nucleus.
source: Neurons strongly immunopositive for CALB2 (CALB2+) were prominent in rostrally in ventral and lateral parts of the fastigial nucleus (vlFN).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Five populations of neurons in the fastigial nucleus were distinguished by their marker gene expression and anatomical distribution.
source: Double-immunostaining revealed five populations of neurons that were distinguished by their marker gene expression and anatomical distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by double-immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neurons that exclusively expressed SPP1 were found in the rostral FN and the rostral DLP.
source: Neurons that exclusively expressed SPP1 were found in two distinct regions: the rostral FN (rFN) (Figure 1E) and the rostral DLP (rDLP).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neurons that coexpressed SPP1 and SNCA were found in the cDLP.
source: In contrast, neurons that coexpressed SPP1 and SNCA (Figure 1H) were found in the cDLP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Neurons that coexpressed SPP1 and SNCA were scattered through the cFN, where they intermingled with a distinct population of neurons which exclusively expressed SNCA.
source: They were also scattered through the cFN, where they intermingled with a distinct population of neurons which exclusively expressed SNCA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: CALB2+ neurons, which were distributed in the vlFN, coexpressed SNCA but not SPP1.
source: CALB2+ neurons (Figure 1G), which were distributed in the vlFN, coexpressed SNCA but not SPP1.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The majority of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei are glutamatergic.
source: Although the majority of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei are glutamatergic, distinct populations of glycinergic and GABAergic neurons have been reported (Fredette and Mugnaini, 1991; Bagnall et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Distinct populations of glycinergic and GABAergic neurons have been reported in the cerebellar nuclei.
source: Although the majority of neurons in the cerebellar nuclei are glutamatergic, distinct populations of glycinergic and GABAergic neurons have been reported (Fredette and Mugnaini, 1991; Bagnall et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Most (93%) of the identified glutamatergic neurons were immunostained by either SPP1 or SNCA.
source: Notably, most (93%; n = 954) of the identified glutamatergic neurons, but none of the GABAergic neurons, were immunostained by either SPP1 or SNCA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: None of the GABAergic neurons were immunostained by either SPP1 or SNCA.
source: Notably, most (93%; n = 954) of the identified glutamatergic neurons, but none of the GABAergic neurons, were immunostained by either SPP1 or SNCA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Glycinergic neurons in the fastigial nucleus comprise two distinct populations.
source: Glycinergic neurons in the FN comprise two distinct populations Bagnall et al., 2009;
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Large glycinergic projection neurons, located ventrally in the rFN, were robustly immunostained by SPP1 (but not SNCA).
source: we found that large glycinergic projection neurons, located ventrally in the rFN, were robustly immunostained by SPP1 (but not SNCA) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: Small glycinergic neurons were not labeled by either SPP1 or SNCA.
source: In contrast, small glycinergic neurons were not labeled by either SPP1 or SNCA (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: The majority of glutamatergic fastigial neurons can be classified into five major types by localization and expression of SPP1, SNCA, and CALB2.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the majority of glutamatergic fastigial neurons can be classified into five major types by localization and expression of SPP1, SNCA, and CALB2.
evidence: This claim is an interpretation of the immunostaining data presented in Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: From an initial pool of 130 randomly harvested fastigial cells, 50 cells were identified as neurons.
source: From an initial pool of 130 randomly harvested fastigial cells, we identified 50 cells which expressed ion channel genes associated with action potentials (Scn8a and Kcna1) and lacked non-neuronal markers (Mobp and Cd68), and were thus considered as neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data.

claim: Most of the identified neurons (84%: 42/50) expressed Slc17a6 (vesicular glutamate transporter 2, VgluT2), indicating that they were glutamatergic.
source: Most of these neurons (84%: 42/50) expressed Slc17a6 (vesicular glutamate transporter 2, VgluT2, Figure 2A), indicating that they were glutamatergic.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Nearly all excitatory neurons (97.6%: 41/42) significantly expressed at least one of the cell-type markers (Spp1, Snca, and Calb2).
source: Nearly all excitatory neurons (97.6%: 41/42) significantly expressed at least one of the cell-type markers (Spp1, Snca, and Calb2), as confirmed with immunostaining in VgluT2-Cre;Ai14 line (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A and immunostaining data.

claim: Hierarchical clustering based on cell-type markers revealed four cell types in the fastigial glutamatergic population, termed F1-F4.
source: Hierarchical clustering based on these markers revealed four cell types in the fastigial glutamatergic population, which we termed F1-F4 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by hierarchical clustering analysis of single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two cell types expressed Spp1 and were distinguished by the absence (F1) or presence (F2) of Snca.
source: Two cell types expressed Spp1 and were distinguished by the absence (F1) or presence (F2) of Snca.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two cell types both expressed Snca and were separated by strong Calb2 expression in F3 but not F4.
source: The other two cell types both expressed Snca and were separated by strong Calb2 expression in F3 but not F4.
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The combinatorial marker expression patterns corresponded with those observed in immunostaining.
source: The combinatorial marker expression patterns corresponded with those observed in immunostaining (Figure 1): F1 with Spp1+ neurons in the rFN (F1R) and the rDLP (F1rDLP), F2 with Spp1+/Snca+ neurons in the cDLP, F3 with Calb2+/Snca+ neurons in the vlFN, and F4 with Snca+ neurons in the cFN.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of single-cell qPCR data (Figure 2A) with immunostaining data (Figure 1).

claim: Nefl, Nefm, and Nefh were highest in F1, intermediate in F2, and lowest in F3 and F4 neurons.
source: Nefl, Nefm, and Nefh were highest in F1, intermediate in F2, and lowest in F3 and F4 neurons (Figure 2A), suggesting that the axon diameter of these cell types are in the order of F1 >F2>F3/F4 (Friede and Samorajski, 1970; Hoffman et al., 1987; Lee and Cleveland, 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The axon diameter of fastigial cell types are in the order of F1 >F2>F3/F4.
source: Nefl, Nefm, and Nefh were highest in F1, intermediate in F2, and lowest in F3 and F4 neurons (Figure 2A), suggesting that the axon diameter of these cell types are in the order of F1 >F2>F3/F4 (Friede and Samorajski, 1970; Hoffman et al., 1987; Lee and Cleveland, 1996).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on neurofilament gene expression data and citations to prior literature on the relationship between neurofilament expression and axon diameter.

claim: Axons from the rFN were thicker than those from the cFN (1.9 ± 0.6 s.d. µm vs 1.0 ± 0.3 s.d. µm).
source: As predicted, axons from the rFN were thicker than those from the cFN (1.9 ± 0.6 s.d. µm vs 1.0 ± 0.3 s.d. µm, n = 30 vs. 25, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by axon diameter measurements from AAV tracing experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Neurofilament expression levels were well correlated with cell body area assessed in immunohistochemically identified fastigial cell types.
source: Neurofilament expression levels were also well correlated with cell body area assessed in immunohistochemically identified fastigial cell types (Nefl in Figure 2B; r2 = 0.996, p=0.002; Nefm and Nefh in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Excitatory projection neurons in the cerebellar nuclei can be distinguished from local interneurons and inhibitory nucleo-olivary neurons by their ability to fire at high rates.
source: Excitatory projection neurons in the cerebellar nuclei can be distinguished from local interneurons and inhibitory nucleo-olivary neurons by their ability to fire at high rates (Uusisaari et al., 2007; Bagnall et al., 2009; Najac and Raman, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Each of the excitatory FN neurons expressed Scn8a (Nav1.6), Scn4b (Navb4), Kcnc1 (Kv3.1), and Syt2 (synaptotagmin 2), as predicted for fast-firing neurons.
source: Each of the excitatory FN neurons expressed Scn8a (Nav1.6), Scn4b (Navb4), Kcnc1 (Kv3.1), and Syt2 (synaptotagmin 2), as predicted for fast-firing neurons (Lien and Jonas, 2003; Mercer et al., 2007; Kodama et al., 2012; Kodama et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data and citations to prior literature.

claim: Variations in neuronal firing capacities can be predicted by the absolute expression levels of fast-spiking genes in vestibular nucleus neurons.
source: Previous studies in vestibular nucleus neurons, which share multiple properties with cerebellar nucleus neurons, including high spontaneous firing rates (Uusisaari et al., 2007; Bagnall et al., 2009; Najac and Raman, 2015) and direct innervation by Purkinje cells (Sekirnjak et al., 2003; Shin et al., 2011), demonstrated that variations in neuronal firing capacities can be predicted by the absolute expression levels of these and other 'fast-spiking' genes (Kodama et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Fastigial cell types F1-F4 exhibited different expression levels of action potential genes Scn8a and Kcnc1, but with an almost constant ratio (r2 = 0.98).
source: Fastigial cell types F1-F4 exhibited different expression levels of action potential genes Scn8a and Kcnc1, but with an almost constant ratio (r2 = 0.98, Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Absolute expression levels of Nefl, Nefm, Nefh, Scn4b, and Syt2 were consistently in the order of F1 >F2>F3/F4.
source: Nefl, Nefm, Nefh, Scn4b, and Syt2 followed the same trend (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G–I); absolute expression levels of these genes were consistently in the order of F1 >F2>F3/F4
evidence: This claim is supported by single-cell qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: F1, F2, and F3 and F4 would have the fastest, intermediate, and the slowest firing capacities.
source: suggesting that F1, F2, and F3 and F4 would have the fastest, intermediate, and the slowest firing capacities.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on gene expression data and prior knowledge about the relationship between gene expression and firing capacity.

claim: Projections from rostral vs caudal fastigial nucleus are known to differ.
source: Although projections from rostral vs caudal fastigial nucleus are known to differ (Angaut and Bowsher, 1970; Bentivoglio and Kuypers, 1982), little is known about the downstream targets of specific fastigial cell types.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Little is known about the downstream targets of specific fastigial cell types.
source: Although projections from rostral vs caudal fastigial nucleus are known to differ (Angaut and Bowsher, 1970; Bentivoglio and Kuypers, 1982), little is known about the downstream targets of specific fastigial cell types.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: Pan-fastigial injections of anterograde tracer revealed divergent fastigial projections to over 60 distinct brain regions.
source: Pan-fastigial injections of anterograde tracer AAV9.hSyn.TurboRFP (Figure 3A) revealed divergent fastigial projections to over 60 distinct brain regions (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—source data 1)
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Projection patterns identified in pan-fastigial injections were quite consistent across individuals.
source: Projection patterns identified in these pan-fastigial injections were quite consistent across individuals (n = 6 males for axonal labeling; n = 4 male and n = 3 female for transsynaptic labeling).
evidence: This claim is supported by the consistency of results across multiple animals.

claim: Fastigial axonal terminals and postsynaptic neurons contralateral to injection sites were prominent in cervical spinal cord, cerebellar cortex, and several regions of the medulla, pons, midbrain, and diencephalon.
source: Fastigial axonal terminals and postsynaptic neurons contralateral to injection sites were prominent in cervical spinal cord (Figure 3C), cerebellar cortex (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F), and several regions of the medulla (Figure 3D), pons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C), midbrain (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), and diencephalon (Figure 3F,G, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde and transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Fastigial projections to the thalamus were not limited to the 'motor thalamus' (VL and VM nuclei), but also robustly to intralaminar thalamus (CL and PF) and the MD nucleus.
source: Notably, fastigial projections to the thalamus were not limited to the 'motor thalamus' (ventrolateral (VL) and ventromedial (VM) nuclei), but also robustly to intralaminar thalamus (centrolateral (CL) and parafascicular (PF)) and the mediodorsal (MD) nucleus (Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde and transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 3F,G and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Fastigial projections were considered to derive from excitatory neurons because inhibitory neurons target different brain regions.
source: These projections were considered to derive from excitatory neurons because inhibitory neurons target different brain regions; glycinergic FN neurons project ipsilaterally, to hindbrain and spinal cord (Bagnall et al., 2009), and GABAergic FN projections exclusively target the IO, as confirmed with selective anterograde tracing by injecting Cre-dependent AAV into the FN of Gad2Cre mice (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on prior literature and confirmed by selective tracing experiments.

claim: Glycinergic FN neurons project ipsilaterally, to hindbrain and spinal cord.
source: glycinergic FN neurons project ipsilaterally, to hindbrain and spinal cord (Bagnall et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GABAergic FN projections exclusively target the IO.
source: and GABAergic FN projections exclusively target the IO, as confirmed with selective anterograde tracing by injecting Cre-dependent AAV into the FN of Gad2Cre mice (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by selective anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Localized injections of AAVs into the rFN, vlFN, and rDLP resulted in differential terminal labeling in several regions of the hindbrain.
source: To distinguish projections from F1R, F3, and F1rDLP, we made localized injections of AAVs into the rFN, vlFN, and rDLP, respectively, which resulted in differential terminal labeling in several regions of the hindbrain, including nucleus reticularis gigantocellularis (NRG), ventral medullary (MdV) and intermediate (IRt) portions of the reticular formation, and inferior vestibular nucleus (IVN) (Figure 4A,B, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Distinct projections from each cell type were confirmed with complementary retrograde tracing experiments.
source: Distinct projections from each cell type were confirmed with complementary retrograde tracing experiments in which FastBlue or retrobeads were injected into NRG/MdV, IVN, and IRt, which are the major projection targets of F1R, F3, and F1rDLP, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: F1R neurons in the rFN made extensive projections to the spinal cord, MdV, NRG, LPGi, IVN, and LVN.
source: Consistent with the known functions of the rostral fastigial nucleus in posture and locomotion (Chambers and Sprague, 1955; Mori et al., 1999), F1R neurons in the rFN made extensive projections to the spinal cord, MdV, NRG, lateral paragigantocellularis (LPGi) (Capelli et al., 2017), IVN, and lateral vestibular nucleus (LVN) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as summarized in Figure 4J and Figure 3—source data 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Axonal terminals of F1R neurons densely innervated the somata and proximal dendrites of huge neurons (diameter >35 µm) in the LVN and NRG.
source: Axonal terminals of F1R neurons densely innervated the somata and proximal dendrites of huge neurons (diameter >35 µm) in the LVN and NRG (Figure 4F), providing a circuit substrate for rapid cerebellar modulation of vestibulospinal, reticulospinal, and reticuloarousal neurons (Eccles et al., 1975a; Eccles et al., 1975b; Wilson and Peterson, 1978).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4F and citations to prior literature.

claim: Brainstem autonomic nuclei implicated in cardiovascular and respiratory functions, including the PMn and LPGi, were targeted by F1R neurons.
source: Brainstem autonomic nuclei implicated in cardiovascular and respiratory functions, including the paramedian nucleus (PMn, Figure 4F; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and LPGi, were also targeted by F1R neurons, as expected from physiological studies in cats (Reis et al., 1973; Bradley et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data and citations to prior literature.

claim: A previously undescribed projection from the rFN to the subcoeruleus region of the dorsal pons was revealed by transsynaptic labeling in tyrosine hydroxylase immunopositive neurons.
source: A previously undescribed projection from the rFN to the subcoeruleus region of the dorsal pons (Figure 4F) was revealed by transsynaptic labeling in tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) immunopositive neurons, which are known to comprise the coeruleospinal pathway (Fung et al., 1991; Jones, 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 4F and citations to prior literature.

claim: The projections of F3 neurons in the vlFN were restricted to the dorsal aspect of the medulla.
source: In contrast with the extensive postsynaptic targets of F1R neurons, the projections of F3 neurons in the vlFN were restricted to the dorsal aspect of the medulla (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), as summarized in Figure 4K and Figure 3—source data 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: F3 neurons project to the Kölliker-Fuse nucleus, which has been implicated in postural and locomotory modulation of respiration.
source: Labeled terminals were identified in the Kölliker-Fuse nucleus (KF; Figure 4G), which has been implicated in postural and locomotory modulation of respiration (Giraudin et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4G and a citation to prior literature.

claim: F3 neurons project to the medial portion of the IVN, which is associated with autonomic function.
source: and in the medial portion of the IVN (Figure 4A), which is associated with autonomic function (McCall et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4A and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Both F1R and F3 neurons project to the IVN, but their postsynaptic targets differ in size and location.
source: Of note, although both F1R and F3 neurons project to the IVN, their postsynaptic targets differ in size and location, with large lateral vs small medial IVN neurons targeted by F1R and F3 neurons, respectively (Figure 4H; somata area, 299 ± 117 s.d. µm2 vs 208 ± 121 s.d. µm2, n = 40 and 44 from two injections each; t(82) = 3.06, p=0.001, Welch's t-test).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: F1rDLP neurons in the rDLP projected to brainstem regions associated with orofacial motor control, including lateral medullary regions (IRt and PCRt) and the facial motor nucleus.
source: F1rDLP neurons in the rDLP projected to the brainstem regions associated with orofacial motor control, including lateral medullary regions (IRt and PCRt; Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and the facial motor nucleus, as summarized in Figure 4L and Figure 3—source data 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Transsynaptic labeling demonstrated that F1rDLP neurons synapse onto CHAT+ neurons in the facial nucleus.
source: Transsynaptic labeling demonstrated that F1rDLP neurons synapse onto CHAT+ neurons in the facial nucleus (Figure 4I), congruent with a previous report demonstrating monosynaptic inputs from the FN to facial motoneurons (Stanek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 4I and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Paired AAV injections targeted to the cDLP and the cFN revealed predominantly non-overlapping fastigial thalamic projections.
source: To distinguish projections from caudally located fastigial cell types, we made paired AAV injections targeted to the cDLP (exclusively F2) and the cFN (predominantly F4, with scattered F2; Figure 1B). These injections revealed predominantly non-overlapping fastigial thalamic projections (Figure 5A); VM, CL, and MD nuclei were innervated by axons originating from the cFN whereas the VL nucleus was innervated by axons from the cDLP.
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: VM, CL, and MD nuclei were innervated by axons originating from the cFN.
source: VM, CL, and MD nuclei were innervated by axons originating from the cFN whereas the VL nucleus was innervated by axons from the cDLP.
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The VL nucleus was innervated by axons from the cDLP.
source: VM, CL, and MD nuclei were innervated by axons originating from the cFN whereas the VL nucleus was innervated by axons from the cDLP.
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Retrogradely labeled neurons from CL and VM injections were found in the cFN and expressed SNCA, confirming their identity as F4.
source: Retrogradely labeled neurons from CL and VM injections were found in the cFN and expressed SNCA (Figure 5B), confirming their identity as F4.
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: VL injections retrogradely labeled neurons in the cDLP that expressed SPP1, confirming their identity as F2.
source: In contrast, VL injections retrogradely labeled neurons in the cDLP that expressed SPP1 (Figure 5C), confirming their identity as F2.
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The F2 module includes brainstem, midbrain, and thalamic nuclei associated with orienting movements of the eyes and head.
source: Localized tracing experiments indicated that F2 neurons in the cDLP projected to midbrain and pontine nuclei associated with orienting movements of the eyes and head, including the superior colliculus (SC), interstitial nucleus of Cajal (INC), caudal pontine reticular formation (PnC), periaqueductal gray (PAG), brainstem nucleus reticularis gigantocellularis (NRG), and cervical spinal cord (Figure 5D and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Projections of F2 neurons were strikingly consistent with those of the fastigial oculomotor region in primates.
source: These projections were strikingly consistent with those of the fastigial oculomotor region in primates (Noda et al., 1990).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison with prior literature.

claim: F2 neurons were retrogradely labeled from localized injections to the PF thalamic nucleus, which is implicated in flexible and goal directed behavior.
source: F2 neurons were also retrogradely labeled from localized injections to the PF thalamic nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), which is implicated in flexible and goal directed behavior (Brown et al., 2010; Bradfield et al., 2013; Kato et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B and citations to prior literature.

claim: F2 neurons were retrogradely labeled from localized injections to the zona incerta, which subserves sensory-motor gating.
source: and the zona incerta (ZI: Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B), which subserves sensory-motor gating (Trageser and Keller, 2004; Mitrofanis, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A,B and citations to prior literature.

claim: F4 neurons projected to several brainstem nuclei associated with arousal and neuromodulation, including the SuM, SNc, LDTg, PTg nuclei, and the NI.
source: F4 neurons projected to several brainstem nuclei associated with arousal and neuromodulation, including the supramammillary region (SuM), substantia nigra pars compacta (SNc), laterodorsal tegmental (LDTg), peduncular tegmental (PTg) nuclei, and the nucleus incertus (NI), as shown in Figure 5E.
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Inputs to SuM, SNc, and LDTg were confirmed with retrograde tracing experiments to originate from F4 neurons.
source: Inputs to SuM, SNc, and LDTg were confirmed with retrograde tracing experiments to originate from F4 neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2C,D.

claim: Transsynaptic labeling from the caudoventral FN indicated that F4 neurons project to both dopaminergic and non-dopaminergic SNc neurons.
source: Transsynaptic labeling from the caudoventral FN, combined with immunostaining for TH, indicated that F4 neurons projection to both dopaminergic (Figure 5E) and non-dopaminergic SNc neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: TH+ neurons in the VTA and RRF were transsynaptically labeled, although fastigial axonal terminals in the VTA were very sparse.
source: TH+ neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), recently shown to mediate cerebellar output for social behavior (Carta et al., 2019), and in the retrorubral field (RRF) were also transsynaptically labeled, although fastigial axonal terminals in the VTA were very sparse (Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D, and a citation to prior literature.

claim: CHAT immunostaining demonstrated that F4 neurons project to both cholinergic and non-cholinergic neurons in the LDTg and PTg.
source: CHAT immunostaining demonstrated that F4 neurons project to both cholinergic and non-cholinergic neurons in the LDTg and PTg (Figure 5E), consistent with observations in primates (Hazrati and Parent, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5E and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Several regions were connected with multiple fastigial cell types.
source: Several regions were connected with multiple fastigial cell types. The brainstem reticular nuclei PnC, NRG, and MdV were targeted by F1R, F1rDLP, and F2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Localized anterograde tracing revealed that fastigial cell types projected to distinct subregions of PnC, NRG, and MdV nuclei.
source: Localized anterograde tracing revealed that fastigial cell types projected to distinct subregions of these nuclei: F2 to dorsal and most medial regions, F1 to more ventral and lateral regions, and F1rDLP projected to dorsal and lateral regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), implying segregation of postsynaptic targets.
evidence: This claim is supported by localized anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Projections to cerebellar cortex and contralateral cerebellar nuclei by each fastigial cell may also be segregated.
source: Projections to cerebellar cortex and contralateral cerebellar nuclei by each fastigial cell may also be segregated as indicated in previous reports (Deura, 1966; Buisseret-Delmas and Angaut, 1989).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on citations to prior literature.

claim: Large Spp1+ F1 neurons in the rFN and rDLP connect with premotor nuclei of the caudal brainstem and spinal cord associated with posture and locomotion, and orofacial motor control.
source: Collectively, these results establish modular connectivity patterns between the fastigial cell types and their downstream targets. Large Spp1+ F1 neurons in the rFN and rDLP connect with premotor nuclei of the caudal brainstem and spinal cord associated with posture and locomotion, and orofacial motor control, respectively.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small Snca+/Calb2+ F3 neurons in the vlFN connect specifically with neurons involved in vestibulo-autonomic and respiratory function.
source: Small Snca+/Calb2+ F3 neurons in the vlFN connect specifically with neurons involved in vestibulo-autonomic and respiratory function.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Medium-large Spp1+/Snca+ F2 neurons in the cDLP connect with pontine, midbrain, and spinal neurons related to orienting movements of the eyes and head and to thalamic nuclei VL and PF.
source: Medium-large Spp1+/Snca+ F2 neurons in the cDLP connect with pontine, midbrain, and spinal neurons related to orienting movements of the eyes and head and to thalamic nuclei VL and PF.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Small Snca+ F4 neurons in the cFN connect with neuromodulatory nuclei of the dorsal pons and midbrain and with 'nonspecific' nuclei of the thalamus including VM, MD, and CL.
source: Small Snca+ F4 neurons in the cFN connect with neuromodulatory nuclei of the dorsal pons and midbrain and with 'nonspecific' nuclei of the thalamus including VM, MD, and CL.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Nonmotor functions of the cerebellum are thought to be mediated largely by cerebellar nucleus linkages with the forebrain.
source: Nonmotor functions of the cerebellum are thought to be mediated largely by cerebellar nucleus linkages with the forebrain (Schmahmann, 1991; Schmahmann, 1996)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Little is known about cell-type specific circuit connections between cerebellar nuclei and the forebrain.
source: but little is known about cell-type specific circuit connections.
evidence: This claim represents a gap in knowledge that the study aims to address.

claim: AAV1.hSyn.Cre injected in the cFN and cDLP of Ai14 mice produced robust transsynaptic axonal labeling in the cerebral cortex.
source: AAV1.hSyn.Cre injected in the cFN and cDLP (F2 and F4 regions) of the fastigial nucleus of Ai14 mice produced robust transsynaptic axonal labeling in the cerebral cortex (Figure 6B–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6B–D and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Two distinct patterns of terminal labeling were observed in the cortex: widespread, diffuse labeling of layer 1 vs localized, specific labeling of layers 3–5.
source: Two distinct patterns of terminal labeling were observed: widespread, diffuse labeling of layer 1 (e.g. layer 1 of secondary motor cortex in Figure 6B, bottom) vs localized, specific labeling of layers 3–5 (e.g. layers 3–5 of motor cortices in Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6B–D.

claim: Layer one terminals were evident throughout much of the cortex, including the sensorimotor, cingulate, insular, prelimbic, frontal association, lateral and ventral orbital, parietal association, and visual cortices.
source: Layer one terminals were evident throughout much of the cortex, including the sensorimotor, cingulate, insular, prelimbic, frontal association, lateral and ventral orbital, parietal association, and visual cortices (Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6E,F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Layer 3–5 terminals were restricted to the sensorimotor cortices, frontal association cortex, and ventral/lateral orbitofrontal cortex.
source: In contrast, layer 3–5 terminals were restricted to the sensorimotor cortices (including somatosensory S1, barrel fields, and S2 and motor regions M1 and M2), frontal association cortex, and ventral/lateral orbitofrontal cortex (Figure 6E,G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6E,G and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: No significant labeling was observed in the infralimbic, medial orbitofrontal, retrosplenial, auditory or temporal cortical areas.
source: We did not observe significant labeling in the infralimbic, medial orbitofrontal, retrosplenial, auditory or temporal cortical areas (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Disynaptic projections from the FN to subcortical forebrain regions were robust in the dorsal striatum.
source: Disynaptic projections from the FN to subcortical forebrain regions were robust in the dorsal striatum (Figure 6C,D,H), consistent with a recent study using rabies virus (Xiao et al., 2018)
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6C,D,H and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Axonal terminals were prominent in the nucleus accumbens of the ventral striatum.
source: Axonal terminals were also prominent in the nucleus accumbens (NAcc) of the ventral striatum (Figure 6I).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Several nuclei of the basal forebrain received disynaptic fastigial input, including the nucleus of the diagonal band of Broca and the medial septum.
source: In addition, several nuclei of the basal forebrain received disynaptic fastigial input, including the nucleus of the diagonal band of Broca (Figure 6J) and the medial septum, which was sparsely but consistently labeled (Figure 6K).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 6J,K.

claim: No evidence was found for either mono- or disynaptic connections between the FN and amygdala or hippocampus.
source: In contrast with early, widely cited reports that suggested relatively direct connections from the vermis to hippocampus and amygdala (Heath and Harper, 1974; Snider and Maiti, 1976), we found no evidence for either mono- or disynaptic connections between the FN and amygdala (Figure 6—figure supplement 1I) or hippocampus.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of labeling in transsynaptic tracing experiments shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Affective and cognitive functions of the vermis could be mediated by fastigial connections with the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and basal forebrain.
source: These results suggest that affective and cognitive functions of the vermis could be mediated by fastigial connections with the cerebral cortex (Figure 6L), basal ganglia (Figure 6M), and basal forebrain.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the connectivity data presented in Figure 6.

claim: Molecularly distinct groups of PCs, arranged in longitudinal stripes distinguished by the expression of Aldolase C, are innervated by specific groups of IO neurons.
source: Molecularly distinct groups of PCs, arranged in longitudinal stripes distinguished by the expression of Aldolase C (Aldoc, aka zebrin II; Figure 7B,C; Sillitoe and Joyner, 2007; Cerminara et al., 2015), are innervated by specific groups of IO neurons which, in turn, are interconnected with regions of the cerebellar nuclei innervated by of the corresponding group of PCs (Ruigrok and Voogd, 1990; Ruigrok and Voogd, 2000; Voogd and Ruigrok, 2004; Sugihara and Shinoda, 2007; Apps and Hawkes, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Injections of tracers restricted to the ventral FN retrogradely labeled PCs confined to narrow, parasagittal bands corresponding with the 1+//1+ and 2+//3+ stripe.
source: Injections of tracers restricted to the ventral FN (F3 region) retrogradely labeled PCs confined to narrow, parasagittal bands; their mediolateral location and immunopositivity for Aldoc indicates that these PCs correspond with the 1+//1+ and 2+//3+ stripe (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B; see Methods for stripe nomenclature).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PCs located in the 1-//1-/2- stripe were retrogradely labeled from rFN.
source: In contrast, PCs located between these bands, in the 1-//1-/2- stripe, were retrogradely labeled from rFN (F1R region) (Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7G and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: rDLP injections retrogradely labeled PCs in the paravermal regions of the simple lobule and Crus II, identified as 2b-//4a- and c-//4b- stripes.
source: rDLP injections (F1rDLP region) retrogradely labeled PCs in the paravermal regions of the simple lobule and Crus II, which were immunonegative for Aldoc and thus identified as 2b-//4a- and c-//4b- stripes (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Injections into the caudalmost portion of the FN retrogradely labeled PCs restricted to the a+//2+ stripe in vermis lobules VI-IX and to the c+//4b+ stripe in Crus I.
source: Injections into the caudalmost portion of the FN, including the cFN (F4 region) and cDLP (F2 region), retrogradely labeled PCs that were restricted to the a+//2+ stripe in vermis lobules VI-IX and to the c+//4b+ stripe in Crus I (Figure 7I).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7I.

claim: Injections of AAV1.hSyn.Cre to label PCs in the medial part of Crus I of Ai14 mice transsynaptically labeled F2 neurons in the cDLP.
source: Injections of AAV1.hSyn.Cre to label PCs in the medial part of Crus I (c+//4b+ region) of Ai14 mice transsynaptically labeled F2 neurons in the cDLP (Figure 7L).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: PC axonal terminals in the F4 region of the cFN were labeled by Cre-dependent AAV injections to lobule VIII in L7Cre mice.
source: In contrast, PC axonal terminals in the F4 region of the cFN were labeled by Cre-dependent AAV injections to lobule VIII in L7Cre mice (Figure 7L).
evidence: This claim is supported by anterograde tracing data shown in Figure 7L.

claim: These connectivity patterns are consistent with results from single axon tracing studies in rats.
source: These connectivity patterns are consistent with results from single axon tracing studies in rats (Sugihara et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on comparison with prior literature.

claim: Pan-fastigial injections of AAV1.hSyn.Cre to Ai14 mice resulted in transsynaptic neuronal labeling throughout the contralateral caudal medial accessory olive and neighboring beta nucleus.
source: Pan-fastigial injections of AAV1.hSyn.Cre to Ai14 mice resulted in transsynaptic neuronal labeling throughout the contralateral caudal medial accessory olive (cMAO) and neighboring beta nucleus (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Each subdivision of the caudal IO was transsynaptically labeled from a specific subregion of the FN.
source: Each subdivision of the caudal IO was transsynaptically labeled from a specific subregion of the FN; injections in the vlFN, rFN and rDLP labeled neurons in the subnuclei a, b, and c of the cMAO, respectively (Figure 7F–H).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 7F–H.

claim: Climbing fibers from cMAO subnuclei a, b, and c innervate PCs associated with the vlFN, rFN, and rDLP, respectively.
source: Notably, climbing fibers from cMAO subnuclei a, b, and c innervate PCs associated with the vlFN (F3 region), rFN (F1R region), and rDLP (F1rDLP region), respectively (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Injections in the cFN transsynaptically labeled neurons in the beta subdivision of the IO, which project to PCs that innervate the cFN.
source: Injections in the cFN transsynaptically labeled neurons in the beta subdivision of the IO (Figure 7K), which project to PCs that innervate the cFN (F4 region) (Sugihara and Shinoda, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 7K and a citation to prior literature.

claim: Injections that included both the cFN and cDLP additionally labeled neurons interposed between beta and subnucleus c which we have termed subnucleus 'd'.
source: Injections that included both the cFN and cDLP additionally labeled neurons interposed between beta and subnucleus c which we have termed subnucleus 'd' (Figure 7J, Figure 7—figure supplement 2, see Methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by transsynaptic tracing data shown in Figure 7J and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: IO neurons in subnucleus d innervate PCs in lobules VIc/VII and Cr I which are linked with cDLP.
source: IO neurons in subnucleus d innervate PCs in lobules VIc/VII and Cr I (Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F) which are linked with cDLP (F2) (Sugihara et al., 2009; Sarpong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F and citations to prior literature.

claim: The excitatory fastigial cell types identified in this study are each linked with a specific group of interconnected PCs and IO neurons.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrate that the excitatory fastigial cell types identified in this study are each linked with a specific group of interconnected PCs and IO neurons (Figure 7M).
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in Figure 7.

claim: Medial cerebellar outputs are mediated by molecularly distinct fastigial cell types which are modularly connected with specific sets of Purkinje cells, inferior olive neurons, and downstream targets.
source: This study demonstrated that medial cerebellar outputs are mediated by molecularly distinct fastigial cell types which are modularly connected with specific sets of Purkinje cells, inferior olive neurons, and downstream targets (Figure 8).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Five major types of glutamatergic projection neurons were identified, which can be divided into two classes.
source: We identified five major types of glutamatergic projection neurons, which can be divided into two classes.
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: Large F1R and F1rDLP neurons, innervated by Aldoc-negative PCs, connect primarily with large brainstem neurons associated with online control of motor and autonomic functions.
source: Large F1R and F1rDLP neurons, innervated by Aldoc-negative PCs, connect primarily with large brainstem neurons associated with online control of motor and autonomic functions.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Smaller F2, F3, and F4 neurons, innervated by Aldoc-positive PCs, connect with multiple downstream circuits associated with sensory processing, motor preparation and arousal.
source: In contrast, smaller F2, F3, and F4 neurons, innervated by Aldoc-positive PCs, connect with multiple downstream circuits associated with sensory processing, motor preparation and arousal.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Each excitatory fastigial cell type receives convergent inputs from widely distributed Purkinje cells associated with a specific set of IO neurons and makes divergent projections to a functionally related collection of downstream targets.
source: Each excitatory fastigial cell type receives convergent inputs from widely distributed Purkinje cells associated with a specific set of IO neurons and makes divergent projections to a functionally related collection of downstream targets.
evidence: This claim is a summary interpretation of the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Diverse functions of the cerebellar vermis are mediated by the parallel operation of several discrete multineuronal circuit modules.
source: These results suggest that diverse functions of the cerebellar vermis are mediated by the parallel operation of several discrete multineuronal circuit modules.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the connectivity data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Specific disynaptic linkages with prefrontal cortex, striatum, basal forebrain, and brainstem arousal circuits made by caudal fastigial neurons could underlie the cognitive and affective disturbances associated with vermal malfunction.
source: Specific disynaptic linkages with prefrontal cortex, striatum, basal forebrain, and brainstem arousal circuits made by caudal fastigial neurons (F2 and F4) could underlie the cognitive and affective disturbances associated with vermal malfunction (Courchesne et al., 1988; Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Badura et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the connectivity data and citations to prior literature.

claim: The fastigial nucleus was known to comprise multiple cell types.
source: Although the fastigial nucleus was known to comprise multiple cell types (Flood and Jansen, 1961; Matsushita and Iwahori, 1971; Beitz and Chan-Palay, 1979; Chen and Hillman, 1993; Ikeda et al., 1995; Bagnall et al., 2009; Chung et al., 2009)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It has been broadly assumed that fastigial outputs are mediated predominantly by large excitatory neurons.
source: it has been broadly assumed that outputs are mediated predominantly by large excitatory neurons.
evidence: This claim represents a prior assumption in the field.

claim: Our findings demonstrate multiple subtypes of glutamatergic projection neurons which vary in size, input-output connectivity, and expression levels of genes associated with fast firing and rapid signal transmission.
source: Our findings demonstrate multiple subtypes of glutamatergic projection neurons which vary in size, input-output connectivity, and expression levels of genes associated with fast firing and rapid signal transmission (Kodama et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is a summary of the main findings of the study.

claim: An additional population of large glycinergic neurons in the rostral fastigial nucleus project ipsilaterally to brainstem nuclei targeted by contralateral F1 excitatory fastigial neurons.
source: An additional population of large glycinergic neurons in the rostral fastigial nucleus project ipsilaterally to brainstem nuclei targeted by contralateral F1 excitatory fastigial neurons (Bagnall et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: GABAergic nucleo-olivary neurons are relatively sparsely distributed in each subregion of the fastigial nucleus.
source: GABAergic nucleo-olivary neurons, abundant in the other cerebellar nuclei (Prekop et al., 2018), are relatively sparsely distributed in each subregion of the fastigial nucleus (Ruigrok and Teune, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Small glutamatergic neurons in the dentate nucleus are located ventrally and are associated with nonmotor functions of the cerebellum.
source: Interestingly, as with fastigial F3 and F4 neurons, small glutamatergic neurons in the dentate (lateral) cerebellar nucleus are located ventrally and are associated with nonmotor functions of the cerebellum (Dum et al., 2002; Küper et al., 2011; Ashmore and Sommer, 2013; Kunimatsu et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The principle that the nervous system minimizes axonal caliber and energy usage suggests that large, fast-spiking cerebellar nucleus neurons may be specialized to meet evolutionarily critical demands.
source: The principle that the nervous system minimizes axonal caliber and energy usage (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Perge et al., 2012; Stevens, 2012) suggests that large, fast-spiking cerebellar nucleus neurons may be specialized to meet evolutionarily critical demands.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on citations to prior literature.

claim: Purkinje cells with the fastest firing capacity (Aldoc-negative) densely innervate the largest fastigial neurons (F1R).
source: Purkinje cells with the fastest firing capacity (Aldoc-negative: Xiao et al., 2014; Zhou et al., 2014) densely innervate the largest fastigial neurons (F1R)
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity data presented in the manuscript and citations to prior literature.

claim: The largest fastigial neurons make extensive synapses onto somata and proximal dendrites of gigantic brainstem neurons responsible for rapid posturomotor reflexes.
source: which in turn make extensive synapses onto somata and proximal dendrites of gigantic brainstem neurons responsible for rapid posturomotor reflexes (Eccles et al., 1975a).
evidence: This claim is supported by the connectivity data presented in the manuscript and a citation to prior literature.

claim: The largest glutamatergic fastigial cell types can transform Purkinje cell synaptic inhibition into precisely timed spikes.
source: The largest glutamatergic fastigial cell types can transform Purkinje cell synaptic inhibition into precisely timed spikes (Özcan et al., 2020), as has been shown for their counterparts in the interpositus and dentate nuclei (Person and Raman, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Physiological properties of the smallest glutamatergic fastigial cell types (F3 and F4) have not been explicitly reported.

source: Inferior olive neurons in the F1rDLP module (cMAO-c) respond to perioral stimuli driven by indirect trigeminal inputs from lateral superior colliculus (Akaike, 1988) and the mesodiencephalic junction (Kubo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior literature.

source: These circuit connections make the F1rDLP module well suited for contextual modulation of trigemino-motor reflexes and the adaptive coordination of multiple oromotor behaviors and breathing.

source: The F3 module includes caudal vestibular nuclei (IVN and MVN), which mediate postural modulation of autonomic functions (Yates, 1996; Yates et al., 2014), the Kölliker Fuse nucleus, which modifies sensory responsiveness of brainstem respiratory circuits (Dutschmann and Herbert, 2006), and the parabrachial complex, thought to be critical for arousal responses to homeostatic distress (Palmiter, 2018).
